title: Anthony Pools v. Sheehan
lead: A diving board retained its identity as a consumer good even within a predominantly construction contract, allowing a warranty claim to return for trial.

actors.name: John and Pilar Sheehan
actors.role: Homeowners who bought a pool and diving board

actors.name: Anthony Pools
actors.role: Designer, builder, and board manufacturer and installer

proceedings: Trial court: directed warranty verdict for Anthony; jury rejected strict liability.
Court of Special Appeals: reversed and ordered a new trial.
Maryland Court of Appeals: affirmed that new-trial judgment on a narrower warranty rationale and adopted the instruction analysis.
limits: The court applied Maryland’s special consumer-warranty statute, not a universal replacement for predominant-purpose analysis. Neither defect, causation, assumption of risk, nor damages was finally determined.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The homeowners buy pool construction and related equipment
sections.cue: Introduce the hybrid bargain and the injury.
paragraphs: John and Pilar Sheehan hired Anthony Pools to design and construct a backyard pool at their Maryland home. Their May 25, 1976 two-sided printed agreement combined retail installment financing with construction. It listed forty-seven specifications or options and required engineering, permits, excavation, steel, gunite, plaster, tile, coping, filtration, and equipment sales. The reverse excluded implied warranties. Prices were not allocated to items or labor, and the documents gave unexplained totals of $7,980 and $9,489.31 before financing charges.

The sixteen-by-forty-foot inground gunite pool ranged from three to eight feet deep, with curved short-side alcoves creating a Grecian shape. Anthony also designed, made, and installed a six-foot diving board centered over the deep-end alcove. Work finished by mid-June. At an August 21 party, John testified that he used the board for the first time, walked toward its pool end after leaving the water, slipped from the right side, and struck the coping.

The Sheehans claimed the skid-resistant material stopped about an inch short of the edges, violating merchantability. They also offered evidence that the board and its placement over the alcove were unreasonably dangerous. These were disputed liability theories, not appellate findings of defect or causation.

sections.title: Two different trial rulings require appellate review
sections.cue: Trace the warranty and strict-liability branches.
paragraphs: At the close of plaintiffs’ evidence, the trial court directed a warranty verdict for Anthony because its express warranties conspicuously excluded others. Strict liability went to the jury, which returned a defense verdict. The Court of Special Appeals reversed for a new trial, treating the pool package as consumer goods with an ineffective disclaimer and finding an omitted instruction about the plaintiff’s conduct.

Anthony obtained review in Maryland’s then-highest court, the Court of Appeals, on warranty, inadvertent use, and contributory negligence as a strict-liability defense. Judge Rodowsky agreed the directed verdict was wrong but took a different warranty route. The Sheehans pressed merchantability under § 2-314, not express warranty or particular-purpose fitness.

sections.title: Construction predominates, but that does not end this statutory inquiry
sections.cue: Explain why the board remains separately important.
paragraphs: Ordinary Article 2 governs goods movable when identified to the contract. Merchantability normally accompanies a merchant’s sale unless validly excluded under § 2-316. Maryland added § 2-316.1: the ordinary exclusion provision did not apply to consumer goods, services, or both, and exclusions of implied consumer warranties or their remedies were unenforceable. Consumer goods were primarily for personal, family, or household use; the statute also preserved sellers’ recourse against manufacturers for resulting warranty damages.

Under the predominant-purpose approach previously adopted in Burton for a landscaping limitations issue, this bargain chiefly bought construction of a reinforced finished pool, not separate purchases of steel, plaster, and tile. Services predominated, and the board was incidental. The court did not simply call the whole undertaking a goods sale. Other pool cases—Gulash, Riffe, Ben Construction, and Chian—illustrated how transaction facts and the particular Article 2 issue affected classification; Chian’s concrete-pool perfect-tender analysis did not resolve this special consumer statute.

The board nevertheless remained distinct. The agreement expressly sold equipment, called the Sheehans buyers, and offered the board as an optional accessory. It was movable when identified, detachable, and not structurally integrated. A separate board purchase would carry merchantability; bundling it with construction needed a reason to eliminate that protection.

sections.title: Maryland’s policy supports warranties on the retained consumer good
sections.cue: State the limited gravamen holding and reservations.
paragraphs: The court considered risk allocation, consumer reliance, and difficulty proving negligence. Newmark, involving lotion supplied with a beauty service, and Worrell, involving a defective fitting furnished with other work, supported attention to the injuring item. Scholar Hawkland’s gravamen approach distinguished defective goods from deficient labor. Those supplied a method, but Maryland’s enactment supplied the decisive policy.

An all-or-nothing classification would eliminate any Article 2 warranty on a good merely because services predominated, frustrating a statute expressly protecting consumer goods and services from warranty exclusions. The court held that when a commercial transaction supplied consumer goods retaining that character after performance, and claimed injury or monetary loss arose from their defect, Maryland implied-warranty rules applied to those goods despite predominant services.

The board met that description, so its merchantability warranty could not be disclaimed. The directed verdict was erroneous. The court reserved goods consumed during a service and whether its limited holding exhausted the statute’s protection for consumer services. It neither abolished predominant-purpose analysis for all purposes nor warranted every service.

sections.title: A new jury must distinguish inadvertence from knowing acceptance of danger
sections.cue: Finish with the adopted instruction analysis and outcome.
paragraphs: For strict liability, the Court of Appeals adopted Part III of the intermediate opinion, reported at 50 Md. App. 614, 620–626. The defense emphasized John’s walking near the edge and turning to speak. Without an instruction, the jury could mistake ordinary carelessness for a complete defense.

Inadvertence, failure to discover a defect, or failure to guard against it did not itself bar strict-liability recovery. Assumption of risk instead required discovery of the defect, actual understanding of its danger, and voluntary, unreasonable encounter with it. That subjective inquiry differed from conduct an ordinarily careful person would avoid. Plaintiffs’ specific request and the defense’s argument required an inadvertence instruction, accompanied by an appropriate assumption-of-risk instruction. Neither appellate court found that John actually assumed the risk.

The Sheehans still had to prove an unreasonably dangerous defect proximately causing injury. On January 25, 1983, the highest court affirmed the new-trial judgment, with costs to Anthony Industries. Both errors supported retrial; it neither affirmed the original defense verdict nor awarded damages. Rodowsky wrote for the six listed judges, with no separate opinion.
